name: HolonIQ on AI in Education: Surveys, National Strategies and Applications
title: HolonIQ on AI in Education: Surveys, National Strategies and Applications
answer: HolonIQ is a market-intelligence platform whose education pages report its own surveys of education executives and its mapping of national AI strategies. Its most useful single finding is that reported successful AI investment and deployment in education rose from 14% in 2019 to 25% in 2022, while the share of organisations with AI merely on the radar fell from 24% to 14%, with testing and assessment expected to feel the greatest impact.

sections.body: HolonIQ publishes market intelligence on the education economy, and the pages read here are its own research notes and reports on artificial intelligence. They include a 2020 landscape mapping 50 national AI strategies, an earlier mapping of 35 strategies that framed a forthcoming AI and Global Education Report, two survey write-ups of its Global Executive Panel, and a blog post on five types of AI in education. The survey work dates from March 2019 and a 2023 update covering 2022, and the strategy landscapes date from 2019 and 2020.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The survey pages trace adoption over time. In 2019, 377 executives from over 25 countries were asked about AI in education. Only one in ten organisations had deployed AI, nearly one in five had completed a pilot, and one in three had no action planned. A lack of clear AI strategy was the biggest barrier, ahead of talent, data and leadership commitment. By 2022, 25% reported successful investment and deployment, up from 14% in 2019, and 44% had AI in short to medium term plans. Machine learning was the most embedded capability at 38%, ahead of natural language processing at 29% and vision at 24%. The most common reason for adopting AI was improving customer outcomes, cited by 75%, against 45% for cost reduction and 43% for market disruption. Testing and assessment was expected to see the greatest impact, followed by language learning, corporate training and higher education. The strategy pages summarise national plans, including Canada's five-year C$125 million Pan-Canadian strategy, China's three-step plan to lead AI by 2030, and Australia's roadmap and projected need for 161,000 additional AI specialist workers by 2030.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: HolonIQ reports that AI deployment in education rose from 14% in 2019 to 25% in 2022, that 44% of respondents had AI in short to medium term plans, and that those with AI only on the radar fell from 24% to 14%. It puts machine learning embedding at 38%, NLP at 29% and vision at 24%. It reports 75% adopting AI to improve customer outcomes, 45% for cost reduction and 43% to disrupt the market. Its 2020 landscape maps 50 national AI strategies covering 90% of global GDP, and it cites McKinsey's estimate of around $13 trillion in additional global economic activity from AI by 2030.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in education can use these pages for two things. The survey series gives a longitudinal read on institutional adoption, barriers and motivations, which is rare in a field where most claims are vendor-led. The strategy landscapes place education and skills commitments inside national AI plans, showing where governments have tied AI to talent development, qualification and training. The applications framework, covering vision, voice, language, algorithms and hardware, gives a working vocabulary for sorting edtech products and claims into categories.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Education

sections.body: The survey findings rest on HolonIQ's own Global Executive Panel rather than a random sample, and the 2019 wave drew 377 respondents, so the percentages describe that panel. The strategy landscapes are dated 2019 and 2020 and several entries describe plans still in draft at the time. The blog post on five types of AI is promotional in part, inviting readers to join the Executive Panel, and the full AI and Global Education Report was offered to paying clients rather than published openly.
